Wish
wish
v. and n. (to desire; the word of Paul's unthinkable prayer for Israel, of the prosperity of the wicked, and of John's greeting to Gaius)
From Old English wyscan, to desire. The Greek at Romans 9:3 is euchomai, to pray or vow — a much stronger word than English wish; at 3 John 2 the same verb governs a greeting.

Biblical Definition

The English word is weak and the Greek behind it is not. Euchomai means to pray or to vow, and Paul uses it for the most extreme statement in his writings: “For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Romans 9:3). He has just finished Romans 8, which ends with nothing being able to separate him from the love of God in Christ, and he opens Romans 9 by saying he could pray to be accursed — anathema — if it would save Israel. The imperfect tense marks it as a wish he knows cannot be granted; Moses had made the same offer, blot me out of thy book. Asaph uses the word of what the wicked appear to have: “Their eyes stand out with fatness: they have more than heart could wish” (Psalm 73:7), in the psalm whose whole argument is that this appearance held until he went into the sanctuary. Paul uses it for the church's maturity, “this also we wish, even your perfection” (2 Corinthians 13:9), and John for a friend: “Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth” (3 John 2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines wish as to have a desire or strong desire, either for what is or is not supposed to be obtainable.

expand to see more

WISH, v.i. To have a desire or strong desire, either for what is or is not supposed to be obtainable.

It usually expresses less than long and covet.

2. To be disposed or inclined to.

WISH, v.t. To desire; to long for; to have a strong desire for.

WISH, n. Desire; sometimes eager desire; longing.

Key Scripture

Romans 9:3 — "For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:"

Psalm 73:7 — "Their eyes stand out with fatness: they have more than heart could wish."

2 Corinthians 13:9 — "For we are glad, when we are weak, and ye are strong: and this also we wish, even your perfection."

3 John 1:2 — "Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth."

Modern Corruption

3 John 2 has been made the charter text of the health-and-wealth message, though it is an ordinary letter greeting with a spiritual measure built into it.

expand to see more

“I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health” is quoted more often than almost any verse in the prosperity movement, and two facts about it are usually withheld. First, the form is the standard health-wish of an ancient letter — the Greek equivalent of I hope this finds you well — and it is John's greeting to one man, Gaius, not a promise to the church. Second, and decisively, it contains its own measure: even as thy soul prospereth. John wishes Gaius bodily prosperity in exact proportion to the state of his soul, which he has just learned is excellent because brethren testified of the truth that was in him. Applied generally, that clause would ruin most of the sermons preached from it.

Romans 9:3 is the passage that shows what Christian desire looks like when it is fully formed, and it runs the other way entirely. Paul, having just declared himself inseparable from Christ, says he could pray to be anathema for his kinsmen. Whether such a wish could be lawful is a question the commentators have long debated; what is beyond debate is what it reveals. The apostle who wrote the most rigorous statement of election in Scripture wrote it out of great heaviness and continual sorrow of heart for those not saved. Any doctrine of election held without that sorrow has been learned from somewhere other than Paul.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek euchomai, to pray or vow — Romans 9:3, 3 John 2, 2 Corinthians 13:9; anathema, accursed — Romans 9:3; Hebrew maskith leb, the imagination of the heart — Psalm 73:7.

expand to see more

Greek euchomai — to pray, to vow; far stronger than English wish; Romans 9:3 and 3 John 2.

Greek anathema — devoted to destruction, accursed; what Paul says he could pray to become.

Greek euodoo — to have a prosperous journey, to prosper; 3 John 2, twice in one verse.

Greek katartisis — perfecting, restoration to order; 2 Corinthians 13:9.

Old English wyscan — to desire; the source of the English word.

Usage

"“I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ” — the Greek is I could pray."

"“Even as thy soul prospereth” — the measure built into the greeting."

"“They have more than heart could wish” — until Asaph went into the sanctuary."
